samples.brief: Online advertorial ('Partner content') for a Bengaluru health-insurance comparison platform on a personal-finance news site, explaining what a super top-up policy is and when salaried 30-45-year-olds supporting retired parents need one; English; 700-900 words; one named advisor quote supplied by the client; soft CTA to the premium calculator; goal: reader understands super top-ups and uses the calculator.
samples.text:
PARTNER CONTENT

Super top-up health insurance: what it covers when a parent's hospital bill outgrows the family policy

For salaried 30-45-year-olds paying for retired parents' healthcare, a super top-up can add large cover behind an existing policy. How the deductible works, and when it is worth buying.

Consider a common Bengaluru household. A 38-year-old software engineer has a Rs 5 lakh family floater through her employer, which covers her, her husband and their daughter. Her parents, both in their late sixties, live with them. Her father has a Rs 3 lakh policy he bought years ago and never increased. When he is admitted for a cardiac procedure, the bill crosses that limit before the discharge papers are ready, and the balance comes out of her savings.

Medical costs rise every year, and parents in their sixties and seventies are the family members most likely to need a hospital stay. Buying a fresh Rs 20 lakh base policy at that age is expensive, and sometimes difficult with existing conditions. A super top-up is one way to raise the ceiling without replacing the policy the family already holds.

What a super top-up is
A super top-up is a health policy that pays only after the family's medical bills in a policy year cross a fixed amount, called the deductible. Below the deductible, the base policy or the policyholder pays. Above it, the super top-up pays, up to its own sum insured.

Because the insurer starts paying only above that threshold, a super top-up usually costs much less than buying the same amount of cover as a base policy. The trade-off is that it is useless on its own for small claims.

Top-up or super top-up: one difference matters
The two names sound alike, but they treat bills differently.
- A regular top-up looks at each hospitalisation separately. If the deductible is Rs 5 lakh and a parent has two admissions of Rs 4 lakh each, neither crosses Rs 5 lakh, so the top-up pays nothing.
- A super top-up adds up all the hospital bills in the policy year. In the same example, the total is Rs 8 lakh, so it pays the Rs 3 lakh above the deductible.

For older parents, who are more likely to be admitted more than once in a year, that aggregate rule is the reason to choose a super top-up over a plain top-up.

When it makes sense
A super top-up is worth considering when:
- the parents already have a base policy, from a past employer or bought years ago, with a sum insured that has not kept up with hospital costs;
- the child's employer cover is the main protection, and it lapses on a job change;
- a new high-value base policy for the parents is unaffordable or hard to get because of their health history;
- the family can pay the deductible from savings or an existing policy, if needed.

It is a poor fit when there is no base cover at all and no savings to bridge the deductible, because every bill below that amount is paid out of pocket.

What to check before buying
Insurance advisors point to five details that decide whether a super top-up pays when it is needed.
1. Match the deductible to the base cover. A Rs 5 lakh deductible sits naturally behind a Rs 5 lakh base policy. A gap between the two is a gap the family pays.
2. Pre-existing conditions. Diabetes, blood pressure and heart conditions are usually covered only after a waiting period. IRDAI's 2024 health-insurance rules cap that waiting period at three years for new policies.
3. Room-rent limits and co-payment. Some policies cap the room category or ask senior policyholders to pay a share of every claim. Both reduce the payout on a large bill.
4. Network hospitals near the parents. Cashless treatment depends on the hospital being in the insurer's network in the city where the parents live.
5. Tax treatment. Under the old tax regime, premiums paid for parents' health insurance, including super top-ups, count toward the Section 80D deduction.

Comparing plans side by side
These details differ from insurer to insurer, and the price for the same cover changes with the parents' ages, city and deductible. [Platform name], a Bengaluru-based health-insurance comparison platform, lists super top-up plans from [N] insurers on one page, with the deductible, waiting periods, room-rent terms and co-payment shown for each.

Its premium calculator asks for the parents' ages, city, existing cover and preferred deductible, and returns quotes from the listed insurers. [Pricing for the buyer, e.g. free to use; to confirm with client.] [Licence line: IRDAI broker / web aggregator registration number, to confirm.]

"[Supplied advisor quote, 1-3 sentences.]" said [Advisor name], [role/credential] at [Platform name].

[Optional sourced proof point, e.g. number of policies issued through the platform in FY2025-26, with source.]

Working out the numbers
The right deductible and sum insured depend on what the family already holds. Readers can estimate super top-up premiums for their parents' ages and city using [Platform name]'s premium calculator [link: rel="sponsored"].

Insurance is the subject matter of solicitation. Read the policy wording, exclusions and terms carefully before buying.

SEO TITLE: [Model name] Review: 21 Days in a Delhi Bedroom
META DESCRIPTION: We ran the Rs 13,000 [Model name] HEPA purifier for 21 days in a 160 sq ft bedroom. PM2.5, noise, filter cost and who should buy the cheaper option.

[Model name] review: 21 days in a Delhi bedroom before the smog season

Disclosure: this article contains Amazon.in affiliate links. If you buy through them, we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. The brand did not see this review before it was published, and our verdict does not depend on which link you click. [Confirm: unit bought by us / loaned by the brand.]

THE SHORT VERDICT
Buy it if: you want one purifier for a child's bedroom or the master bedroom, up to about 160 sq ft, and you can budget roughly Rs 4,200-5,600 a year for filters.
Skip it if: you need to clean a large living room, your router only gives you a 5 GHz network, or the running cost matters more to you than speed.
Price: Rs 13,000 on Amazon.in (checked [date]).
Our score: [X/10]
[Check the price on Amazon.in -> affiliate link]

HOW WE TESTED IT
We ran the [Model name] for 21 days in a 160 sq ft bedroom in [locality, Delhi-NCR] in [month, year], with the windows shut and the door closed during tests. We measured PM2.5 with [monitor model] placed [distance] from the purifier at bed height, and noise with [sound meter] at [distance]. Each speed test started with the room's air as it was that evening; we did not light anything to push the reading up. On most days the purifier ran on high for the first hour after we came home and on [lower setting] overnight. [Photo: purifier in the test bedroom.] [Photo: monitor reading before and after.]

WHAT IT DOES WELL
It clears a bedroom fast. On high, PM2.5 in the test room fell from about 180 to 35 in 40 minutes. For context, India's national 24-hour standard for PM2.5 is 60 µg/m³, so 180 is three times that limit: the kind of reading Delhi flats see on bad winter evenings. Forty minutes is roughly the time between a child's bath and bedtime. Switch it on when you get home, close the door, and the room is in much better shape by the time the lights go off.

It holds the room once it gets there. Over the 21 days, overnight readings stayed [range, from tester notes] on the lower setting as long as the door stayed shut. The practical lesson: a purifier can only clean the air it can reach. In a flat where the bedroom door stays open to the hall, expect slower numbers than ours.

High is loud, but usable. We measured 52 dB on high. You will notice it: it is audible over a quiet conversation. It is fine while you read or put the children to bed, and most families will want to drop it to a lower setting for sleep once the room is clean. [Tester note to confirm: dB on the lowest setting.]

The app is useful once it is connected. [Tester note to confirm: what the app shows (live PM2.5, filter life, schedules) and whether schedules worked reliably over 21 days.]
A schedule that starts the purifier half an hour before you get home is the most useful thing it can do in a Delhi winter.

WHERE IT FALLS SHORT
The filter is the real price. A replacement filter costs Rs 2,800 and lasts 6-8 months, depending on how hard you run it. In a Delhi winter, assume the shorter end. That is Rs 4,200-5,600 a year, or Rs 12,600-16,800 over three years: more than the purifier itself. This is the con that matters most to families on a budget, and the main reason to look at the cheaper alternative below. Before you buy, check that the filter is in stock on Amazon.in and on the brand's own store. A purifier without a filter you can buy is a box with a fan.

The app needs 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. Many newer routers combine 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz under one network name, and app setup can fail on those. The fix is to split the bands in your router settings, or to set up the purifier from a phone hotspot running on 2.4 GHz. It took us [time, from tester notes] to get connected. If you are not comfortable changing router settings, use the buttons on the unit and skip the app, or ask someone who is.

One room only. We tested in a 160 sq ft room, and that is the size we can vouch for. The brand rates it for [rated coverage from the spec sheet]. We did not test it in a larger living room; expect it to take much longer there.

HOW IT COMPARES
[Cheaper alternative model], Rs [price] on Amazon.in (checked [date]). Pick this if your budget is the limit or the filter cost puts you off. [From tests or the spec sheet: CADR, filter price and life, noise.]
The trade-off is [slower cleaning / no app / louder], which matters less in a small bedroom where you can switch it on an hour before bedtime. [Check the price on Amazon.in -> affiliate link]

The [Model name] is the better pick if you want the room clean soon after you walk in, or if you want the app's schedules and filter alerts.

BUYING ADVICE
- Size it to the room you will actually use it in. For a bedroom of about 160 sq ft, the [Model name] is enough. For a living room, look at a larger model rather than running this one on high all day.
- Count the filter, not just the box. The real first-year cost is Rs 13,000 plus about Rs 4,200-5,600 in filters.
- Check warranty and service. [Warranty term, and whether service in Delhi-NCR is on-site or carry-in; to confirm with the brand.] Keep the invoice from your Amazon.in order.
- Buy before the season. Popular purifiers and their filters tend to go out of stock once the AQI is in the news. Buying in October gives you time to set it up and learn the settings.
- Look for a true HEPA filter in the specification, not 'HEPA-type' wording. [Confirm the filter grade from the spec sheet.]

QUESTIONS PARENTS ASK
Is it safe to run in a baby's room overnight?
A HEPA purifier cleans air by pushing it through a filter. [Confirm from the spec sheet whether the model has an ioniser and whether it can be switched off.]
Keep the unit where a crawling child cannot reach the controls, and use a lower setting at night so the noise does not wake them.

Can I wash the filter to make it last longer?
Do not wash a HEPA filter unless the manual says you can; water can damage the filter material. Some purifiers have a washable pre-filter in front of the HEPA layer that catches dust and hair. [Confirm whether this model has one.]

Should I keep the windows closed?
While it runs, yes. A purifier cannot keep up with outside air coming in through an open window. Air the room on cleaner afternoons and close the windows before you switch it on.

Will it help with Diwali smoke?
It will bring PM2.5 down in a closed room once the smoke outside settles, the same way it did in our test. For smells, check whether the model has an activated-carbon layer. [Confirm from the spec sheet.]

Does it need to run all day?
No. In our test it took 40 minutes on high to clean the room. Run it on high when you come in, then lower it overnight. Running it less also stretches the filter towards the 8-month end.

FINAL VERDICT
If you want one bedroom in a Delhi flat cleaned quickly every evening this winter, the [Model name] does that. In our 160 sq ft test room, PM2.5 fell from about 180 to 35 in 40 minutes. Budget for its filters before you buy. If that running cost is too much, the [Cheaper alternative model] is the sensible step down.

[Buy the [Model name] on Amazon.in -> affiliate link]
[See the [Cheaper alternative model] on Amazon.in -> affiliate link]
(All affiliate links carry rel="sponsored".)

[Theme line of the report, to recur here and in the CEO review: e.g. "Building through the cycle"]

Dear Shareholders,

FY2025-26 was a year in which your company sold more than ever before and earned less on each rupee it sold. I want to explain both halves of that sentence plainly, because you are entitled to the whole account, not only the good part of it.

The year in numbers
Revenue rose 11% to Rs 2,140 crore. [VERIFY vs audited FS, p. __] Volumes grew in [CONFIRM: segments / export markets that drove growth], and customers who had paused orders in the previous year returned. That growth is real, and it came from products and customers we have spent years building.

Our EBITDA margin, however, fell from 18% to 15%. [VERIFY vs audited FS, p. __] On these figures, EBITDA was roughly Rs 321 crore against about Rs 347 crore last year. [VERIFY: derived figures; replace with audited EBITDA.] The main cause was the cost of raw materials, [CONFIRM: which inputs, e.g. key feedstocks and solvents], which rose faster than we could pass on to customers. Many of our contracts reset prices [CONFIRM: quarterly / half-yearly], so for part of the year we were selling at prices agreed before our costs went up. We do not regard that as bad luck to be waited out. It is a weakness in how our contracts are written, and we are fixing it.

What we are doing about margins
Over the year, the management team [CONFIRM: actions taken, e.g. moved a larger share of contracts to formula-based pricing linked to input costs, qualified additional suppliers for key inputs, and reduced energy use per tonne at existing plants]. Some of these steps show results within a quarter; others take a full contract cycle. I would rather tell you that now than promise a quick recovery the numbers may not deliver. Your Managing Director sets out the detail, and the targets, in the review that follows.

Dahej: late, and what we learned
The new plant at Dahej was commissioned during the year, six months later than we told you it would be. [CONFIRM: commissioning month.] The delay was caused by [CONFIRM: cause, e.g. equipment deliveries, approvals, contractor performance]. It cost us [CONFIRM: what the delay cost, e.g. the revenue the plant would have earned in those months, and any cost overrun against the approved budget].

Your Board reviewed the project at each of its meetings during the delay. Two lessons have changed how we will build from now on. First, [CONFIRM: lesson one, e.g. ordering long-lead equipment before final approvals]. Second, [CONFIRM: lesson two, e.g. a commissioning schedule with independent review at each milestone]. The plant is now running at [CONFIRM: utilisation] and will contribute through FY2026-27. I will report its progress to you in next year's letter against the targets in the MD's review.

Sustainability, now checked by someone else
This year, for the first time, our sustainability report has been externally assured by [CONFIRM: assurance provider, standard and level of assurance]. That matters for a simple reason. Until now, you had our word on our energy use, emissions, water and safety numbers. Now an independent assurer has checked them before you read them. Several of our largest customers, particularly in export markets, ask for exactly this before they place long-term orders. [CONFIRM: any customer or market requirement the company can name.] The full report is at [link / page reference].

Dividend
Your Board has recommended a dividend of Rs [__] per share, the same as last year. [VERIFY vs Board resolution.] In a year when profits per rupee of sales fell, we considered this carefully. We kept the dividend unchanged because [CONFIRM: reasoning, e.g. the balance sheet and cash flows support it while Dahej's capital spending is largely behind us], and because we want shareholders to be able to plan on it.

Governance and people
[CONFIRM: board changes during the year, e.g. new independent directors, retirements, with names and roles.] I thank [CONFIRM: retiring director's name] for [CONFIRM: years] years of service on this Board.

I also want to thank the teams at our plants, and especially those at Dahej, who worked through a long and difficult start-up. A late project is hard on the people building it, and they finished the job. [CONFIRM: safety record for the year, e.g. lost-time injury figure, as reported in the assured sustainability report.]

What we told you last year, and how we did
In last year's report we set out [CONFIRM: number] priorities. [CONFIRM: list each priority with a one-line result, e.g. "Commission Dahej: done, six months late", "Grow exports to X% of revenue: achieved / not achieved".] Where we fell short, I have said so above.

Looking ahead
Our priorities for FY2026-27 are clear. We will recover margin by changing how we price, not by hoping input costs fall. We will bring Dahej to [CONFIRM: utilisation target, if cleared by legal] and earn a return on the money you invested in it. And we will keep our sustainability numbers externally assured, so that you and our customers can rely on them.

The specialty-chemicals cycle will not always run in our favour. What we can control is how we price our products, how we build plants and what we tell you about both. This letter is my account of a mixed year. I hope it gives you reason to trust the next one.

With regards,

[Name]
Chairman
[Place], [Date]

samples.brief: API reference page for 'Create a refund' (POST /v1/payments/{payment_id}/refunds) of a Bengaluru payment gateway: full and partial refunds in paise, Idempotency-Key header, optional notes object, 4 errors (payment not captured, amount exceeds captured, duplicate idempotency key with different body, refund window expired); audience: backend developers at Indian D2C merchants; English; 300-600 words plus a curl example and JSON request/response; goal: a correct first refund call.
samples.text:
Create a refund

POST /v1/payments/{payment_id}/refunds

Creates a full or partial refund for a captured payment. Money moves back to the customer's original payment method, and the refund amount is deducted from your next settlement. You can make several partial refunds against one payment until the captured amount is used up.

Authentication and headers
- Authorization: Basic auth with your key ID as the username and key secret as the password. Use your test keys in test mode.
- Idempotency-Key (required): a unique string of up to [64] characters, such as a UUID. If a request times out, retry it with the same key and the same body; you get the original refund back instead of a second refund.
- Content-Type: application/json

Path parameters
| Name | Type | Required | Description |
| payment_id | string | Required | ID of the captured payment to refund, for example pay_9AbCdEfGh123. |

Body parameters
| Name | Type | Required | Description |
| amount | integer | Optional | Amount to refund, in paise. 10000 = Rs 100.00. Must be at least 100 (Rs 1) and no more than the captured amount minus earlier refunds. Leave it out to refund the full remaining amount. |
| notes | object | Optional | Your own key-value pairs, such as an order ID or reason. Up to [15] keys; each value up to [256] characters. Returned unchanged in the response and in webhooks. |

Example request
curl -X POST https://api.[gateway].com/v1/payments/pay_9AbCdEfGh123/refunds \
  -u [YOUR_TEST_KEY_ID]:[YOUR_TEST_KEY_SECRET] \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 6f1c2a7e-3b4d-4e8f-9a10-2c5d7e9b1f34" \
  -d '{
    "amount": 49900,
    "notes": {
      "order_id": "ORD-10432",
      "reason": "Size exchange not available"
    }
  }'

This refunds Rs 499.00 of the payment. To refund the whole remaining amount, send the same request without "amount".

Response
201 Created. Returns the refund object.
| Field | Type | Description |
| id | string | Refund ID, prefixed rfnd_. |
| entity | string | Always "refund". |
| payment_id | string | The payment this refund belongs to. |
| amount | integer | Refunded amount, in paise. |
| currency | string | ISO 4217 code. Always "INR" for domestic payments. |
| status | string | pending, processed or failed. Most refunds start as pending. |
| notes | object | The notes you sent, or an empty object. |
| created_at | integer | Unix timestamp, in seconds. |

{
  "id": "rfnd_7XyZaBcDeF456",
  "entity": "refund",
  "payment_id": "pay_9AbCdEfGh123",
  "amount": 49900,
  "currency": "INR",
  "status": "pending",
  "notes": {
    "order_id": "ORD-10432",
    "reason": "Size exchange not available"
  },
  "created_at": 1791187200
}

A pending refund has been accepted, not yet credited. Listen for the refund.processed and refund.failed webhooks instead of polling.

Errors
| HTTP status | Code | What it means | How to fix it |
| 400 | PAYMENT_NOT_CAPTURED | The payment is authorized but not captured, so there is nothing to refund. | Capture the payment first, or void the authorization if you do not want to charge the customer. |
| 400 | AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_CAPTURED | amount is more than the captured amount minus earlier refunds. | Fetch the payment, read amount_refunded, and send a value no larger than the remaining amount. Check that you sent paise, not rupees. |
| 409 | IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED | You reused an Idempotency-Key with a different request body. | Use a new key for a new refund. Reuse a key only to retry the identical request. |
| 400 | REFUND_WINDOW_EXPIRED | The payment is older than the refund window of [N] days. | Refund the customer outside the gateway, for example by bank transfer, and record it in your own system. |

Every error response has the shape {"error": {"code": "...", "description": "..."}}.

Notes
- Amounts are always in paise, in requests, responses and webhooks.
- A refund cannot be cancelled once created.
- Rate limit: [N] requests per second per key; on HTTP 429, retry with backoff using the same Idempotency-Key.

Related: Fetch a payment, Fetch refunds for a payment, Refund webhooks, Idempotency guide, Changelog.

SHORT DESCRIPTION (80): Split rent, groceries and trip costs with friends. Settle up on UPI in one tap.

SCREENSHOT CAPTIONS
1. Flat ka hisaab, bina jhagde ke
2. Kisko kitna dena hai, ek nazar mein
3. Item se split karo ya share se
4. Ek tap mein UPI request bhejo
5. Rent ki date? Hum yaad dilayenge

FULL DESCRIPTION
[Brand] keeps track of who paid for what in your flat or on your next college trip, then lets everyone settle up on UPI. No more spreadsheets, no more "bhai, kitne hue?" in the group chat.

Add an expense when you pay. [Brand] works out each person's share and keeps a running total, so anyone in the group can see who owes whom.

WHAT YOU CAN DO
- Split by item or by share. Pay the grocery bill and assign each item to the person who used it, or split by fixed shares, like a bigger share for the person with the bigger room.
- Settle up on UPI. Send a UPI request for exactly what someone owes. They pay from the UPI app they already use, and the balance updates.
- Get monthly rent reminders. Set the rent date once. Everyone in the flat gets a reminder before it's due, so no one has to chase.
- Use it in Hindi or English. Switch the app's language any time; your groups and expenses stay the same.

MADE FOR
- Flatmates sharing rent, Wi-Fi, maid and groceries every month.
- College trips where one person books the hostel, another pays for the cab and someone else covers dinner.
- Any group that is tired of keeping the hisaab in their heads.

YOUR MONEY STAYS IN YOUR UPI APP
Payments happen in your own UPI app. [Brand] sends the request and records the payment; it never holds your money. [CONFIRM with product and legal: payment flow, data stored, and any partner bank or PSP named in the listing.] Read how we handle your data in our privacy policy: [link].

Start with your next shared bill. Create a group, add your flatmates or trip gang, and log the first expense.

WHAT'S NEW
[Version x.x]: [The one change users will notice in this release, in one line. Never 'bug fixes and improvements'.]

Many of you ordered these boxes for a specific evening: a puja, a visit to your parents, a gift for someone you couldn't see in person. Some of those evenings passed without the sweets. Others called us for hours and heard nothing. That is on us, not on the courier.

What we have done:
- On [date], we refunded the delivery fee on every late order to the original payment method. You don't need to ask for it.
- On [date], we added a second courier partner, so no single partner carries all our orders.

What changes:
- Until the festive season ends, we will take orders for each delivery date only up to what both couriers can carry. [CONFIRM capacity rule.]
- From [date], [CONFIRM: support change, e.g. support hours and staffing during festival weeks]. I am personally accountable for both changes.

If your box arrived late or damaged, email [support email] or WhatsApp [number] with your order number by [date]. We will [CONFIRM: replace the box or refund the order] within [N] working days.

[Founder name]
Founder and CEO, [Brand]

samples.text:
सगाई की रात | एपिसोड 1: हिसाब बराबर
किरदार:
- मेहर अवस्थी (26)
- हरिओम अवस्थी (मेहर के पापा, 58, जाजमऊ में छोटी टैनरी)
- सुधा (मेहर की माँ)
- चिंकी (मेहर की चचेरी बहन, 19)
- कबीर मल्होत्रा (मंगेतर, 28)
- राजेश्वर मल्होत्रा (कबीर के पापा, 60)

[COLD OPEN. 2012. Night. Rain on a tin roof. A landline rings in an old house. Small footsteps run across a stone floor. The receiver is picked up.]

मेहर (12 साल की, नींद में): हैलो? अवस्थी जी का घर।

[A man's voice on the line, calm, almost friendly. Under it, a slow metallic tapping: tak... tak... tak, a ring on a glass.]

आदमी: बिटिया, पापा सो गए?

मेहर: जी... आप कौन?

आदमी: पापा को बस इतना बोल देना। कल सुबह बैंक वाले आएँगे।

[Tak... tak... tak.]

आदमी: और बोलना, हिसाब बराबर।

[He laughs once, short and low. The line goes dead. Dial tone. Behind Mehar, a door opens.]

हरिओम (दूर से, घबराया हुआ): मेहर! किसका फ़ोन था? मेहर, किसका फ़ोन था?

[The dial tone stretches and distorts into a dhol beat. Music: title theme, 10 seconds.]

[SCENE 1. Present day. Kanpur, a lawn in Civil Lines. Dhol, shehnai, a crowd laughing. A door shuts and the noise drops. A small dressing room. Bangles, a hairdryer switching off.]

चिंकी: दीदी, हिलो मत! एक झुमका और बाक़ी है।

मेहर: चिंकी, साढ़े सात बज गए। मल्होत्रा अंकल अब तक पहुँचे कि नहीं?

चिंकी: पहुँच गए! दुबई से सीधा। गाड़ी से उतरते ही मौसा जी से गले मिले।

मेहर: पापा से? पापा ठीक लग रहे थे?

चिंकी: ठीक का तो पता नहीं। पसीना बहुत आ रहा था उन्हें। एसी वाले हॉल में।

[Her phone buzzes. A WhatsApp call tone.]

चिंकी: कबीर जीजू! उठाओ, उठाओ।

[Mehar picks up. Kabir's voice through the phone speaker, warm, slightly breathless.]

कबीर: मेहर, एक मिनट है तुम्हारे पास?

मेहर: तीस सेकंड। चिंकी झुमका लेकर खड़ी है।

कबीर: बस इतना बताना था। पापा आ गए हैं। पहली बार तुमसे मिलेंगे।

मेहर: डर लग रहा है, कबीर। वीडियो कॉल पर तो उन्होंने कभी कुछ बोला ही नहीं।

कबीर: वो ऐसे ही हैं। कम बोलते हैं, पर जब बोलते हैं तो पूरा हॉल सुनता है।

मेहर: वाह। बहुत तसल्ली मिली।

कबीर (हँसते हुए): अरे सुनो। अंगूठी वाले टाइम पर मेरी तरफ़ देखना। बस। बाक़ी सब मैं सँभाल लूँगा।

[Call ends. A short silence. Distant dhol.]

चिंकी: दीदी, तुम मुस्कुरा रही हो।

मेहर: चुप। झुमका लगा।

[SCENE 2. The lawn. Live band playing an old Hindi film tune. Crowd chatter. A mic thumps. Sudha's voice, close, low.]

सुधा: मेहर, इधर आओ बेटा। सीधे स्टेज पर नहीं, पहले पापा के पास।

मेहर: मम्मी, पापा कहाँ हैं?

सुधा: वहीं, बार के पास। दो बार पानी माँग चुके हैं। तुम बस उनका हाथ पकड़ लेना।

मेहर: मम्मी, सब ठीक तो है न?

सुधा: सब ठीक है। बस... आज उन्होंने वो पुरानी घड़ी पहनी है।

मेहर: कौन-सी?

सुधा: वही, सुनहरी वाली। जो बड़ी टैनरी के उद्घाटन पर पहनी थी। चौदह साल से अलमारी में बंद थी।

मेहर: आज क्यों?

सुधा: पूछा था। बोले, आज का दिन उस दिन से बड़ा है।

[Footsteps on grass. The band fades under.]

मेहर: पापा?

हरिओम: आ गई मेरी बिटिया। (a breath) बहुत सुंदर लग रही हो, मेहर।

मेहर: आपका हाथ ठंडा क्यों है, पापा?

हरिओम: कुछ नहीं। बूढ़ा हो गया हूँ। चलो, लोग इंतज़ार कर रहे हैं।

[SCENE 3. The stage. A mic is tapped twice. Feedback squeal, quickly cut. The crowd goes quiet.]

एंकर: लेडीज़ एंड जेंटलमेन, अंगूठी की रस्म से पहले, दूल्हे के पिता, श्री राजेश्वर मल्होत्रा जी, दो शब्द कहना चाहते हैं।

[Applause. Heavy, unhurried footsteps on the wooden stage. Then a sound Mehar has not heard in fourteen years: a ring tapping on a glass. Tak... tak... tak.]

[Music: a single low cello note enters and holds.]

राजेश्वर: नमस्कार। मैं ज़्यादा बोलता नहीं हूँ, ये कबीर आपको बता चुका होगा।

[Light laughter in the crowd.]

राजेश्वर: बस इतना कहूँगा। कानपुर से मेरा पुराना रिश्ता है। बहुत पुराना।

[Tak... tak... tak.]

राजेश्वर: और आज लगता है कि ज़िंदगी ने वो रिश्ता पूरा कर दिया। तो अवस्थी जी... (a short, low laugh) हिसाब बराबर।

[The cello note cuts out. The 2012 dial tone bleeds in under the crowd's applause, then the child's voice, echoing.]

मेहर (12 साल की, echo): पापा, किसका फ़ोन था?

[A glass shatters on a stone floor. The applause falters. Murmurs.]

सुधा: (sharp whisper) हरिओम जी!

हरिओम: (too loud) कुछ नहीं, कुछ नहीं! हाथ से फिसल गया। आप लोग जारी रखिए।

कबीर (close, a whisper): मेहर? मेहर, तुम ठीक हो? तुम काँप रही हो।

मेहर: कबीर... तुम्हारे पापा... ये ग्लास पर अंगूठी से टक-टक... ये हमेशा करते हैं?

कबीर: हाँ, बचपन से। क्यों?

मेहर: (barely audible) कुछ नहीं। मुझे दो मिनट चाहिए। बस दो मिनट।

[SCENE 4. A service corridor behind the kitchen. Steel utensils clanging, a cook shouting for more naan. The band is muffled through a wall. Fast footsteps behind Mehar.]

कबीर: मेहर, रुको! कहाँ जा रही हो? पंडित जी बुला रहे हैं।

मेहर: वॉशरूम, कबीर। बस आ रही हूँ।

कबीर: वॉशरूम दूसरी तरफ़ है। ये रास्ता छत पर जाता है।

[Mehar stops. The kitchen noise carries on around them.]

मेहर: कबीर, एक बात पूछूँ? सच बताना।

कबीर: पूछो।

मेहर: तुम्हारे पापा पहले कभी कानपुर आए हैं?

कबीर: हाँ, बहुत पहले। मैं स्कूल में था। कुछ साल लेदर का बिज़नेस किया था उन्होंने यहाँ।

मेहर: लेदर का?

कबीर: हाँ। फिर एक डील के बाद सब छोड़कर दुबई चले गए। कहते हैं, उस एक डील ने उनकी ज़िंदगी बना दी।

[A pan crashes somewhere in the kitchen. Mehar flinches.]

कबीर: मेहर? तुम्हारी आवाज़ काँप रही है। क्या हुआ?

मेहर: कुछ नहीं। तुम नीचे जाओ, कबीर। पंडित जी से कहो, पाँच मिनट।

कबीर: मैं तुम्हारे साथ चलता हूँ।

मेहर: नहीं! (softer) प्लीज़। पाँच मिनट।

[Kabir's footsteps walk away, slowly, then stop.]

कबीर (from a distance): मेहर। जो भी है, मुझे बताओगी न?

[No answer. Mehar's footsteps start up the stairs.]

[SCENE 5. A staircase. The party noise falls away floor by floor. A metal door creaks open onto the roof. Wind, a far-off train horn, traffic on the Ganga bridge.]

मेहर: पापा।

[Silence. A matchstick strikes. Someone exhales.]

मेहर: आपने बीस साल पहले सिगरेट छोड़ दी थी।

हरिओम: छोड़ दी थी। आज एक पी लेने दो, मेहर।

मेहर: वो आवाज़। वो टक-टक। मैं बारह साल की थी पापा, पर मुझे याद है।

हरिओम: मुझे पता था तुम्हें याद होगा। उसके बाद तुम दो रात ठीक से सोई नहीं थीं।

मेहर: वो आदमी राजेश्वर मल्होत्रा है?

[A long pause. The train horn again, closer.]

हरिओम: हाँ।

मेहर: क्या किया था उसने?

हरिओम: अवस्थी टैनरी याद है? जाजमऊ वाली, बड़ी। तीन सौ लोग काम करते थे।

मेहर: याद है।

हरिओम: उसने इटली का एक ऑर्डर दिलवाया। सबसे बड़ा ऑर्डर। मैंने बैंक से लोन लेकर माल बनाया।

मेहर: फिर?

हरिओम: माल उसकी कंपनी के नाम से गया। पेमेंट उसके पास आया। मेरे पास आया बैंक का नोटिस।

मेहर: और आपने पुलिस में...

हरिओम: हर काग़ज़ पर मेरे दस्तख़त थे, मेहर। उसके नहीं। मैंने ख़ुद पढ़े बिना साइन किए थे।

मेहर: क्योंकि आप उस पर भरोसा करते थे।

हरिओम: दोस्त था। पाँच साल से साथ उठना-बैठना था। तुम्हारे नामकरण पर भी आया था।

मेहर: फिर क्या हुआ? उस फ़ोन के बाद?

हरिओम: अगली सुबह बैंक वाले आए। फ़ैक्ट्री पर ताला लगा। तीन सौ लोगों की तनख़्वाह रुकी।

मेहर: वो घर? स्वरूप नगर वाला?

हरिओम: वो भी गया। तुम्हारी मम्मी के गहने भी। तुम्हें लगता था हम किराए के घर में शौक़ से आए थे।

मेहर: मैंने कभी पूछा भी नहीं, पापा।

हरिओम: मैंने पूछने भी नहीं दिया। दस साल लगे दोबारा एक छोटी यूनिट खड़ी करने में। चालीस लोग। बस।

[Her phone buzzes. A message tone, twice.]

मेहर: कबीर का मैसेज है। "सब ठीक? पापा तुम्हें ढूँढ रहे हैं।"

हरिओम: (a dry laugh) ढूँढ रहे हैं। चौदह साल बाद।

[Wind. Sudha's footsteps on the stairs, fast.]

सुधा: मेहर! हरिओम जी! नीचे सब पूछ रहे हैं। पंडित जी मुहूर्त निकल जाने की बात कर रहे हैं।

मेहर: मम्मी, आपको पता था?

[Silence.]

सुधा: (quietly) तुम्हारे पापा ने आज शाम बताया। जब उनकी गाड़ी आई।

मेहर: आज शाम? मम्मी, ये रिश्ता चार महीने से चल रहा है!

[SCENE 6. The roof. Mehar's breathing, fast. Her bangles rattle as she pulls at them.]

मेहर: ठीक है। मैं नीचे जा रही हूँ। माइक पर सबके सामने बोलूँगी कि ये सगाई नहीं होगी।

हरिओम: नहीं।

मेहर: नहीं? पापा, उस आदमी ने हमारी ज़िंदगी...

हरिओम: मैंने कहा, नहीं।

[The cigarette is ground out under a shoe.]

हरिओम: ये सगाई होगी, मेहर। आज रात। सबके सामने।

मेहर: आप... आप ये कैसे कह सकते हैं?

हरिओम: क्योंकि ये रिश्ता किस्मत से नहीं आया, बिटिया।

[Music: the low cello note returns, building.]

हरिओम: कबीर का बायोडेटा उस रिश्ते वाली आंटी तक मैंने पहुँचाया था। चार महीने पहले।

मेहर: (a breath) क्या?

हरिओम: चौदह साल से मैं इसी रात का इंतज़ार कर रहा था।

[From the stairwell, slow heavy footsteps climbing. Then, close to the roof door: tak... tak... tak.]

राजेश्वर (off, calm, friendly): अवस्थी जी? ऊपर हैं क्या? बेटी को ढूँढ रहा था मैं।

[Music cuts to silence.]

[TAG. Narrator, low and close.]

नैरेटर: एक पिता, जिसने चौदह साल हिसाब रखा। एक बेटी, जिसे आज पता चला कि उसकी सगाई भी उसी हिसाब का हिस्सा है। अगले एपिसोड में: हरिओम अवस्थी का प्लान क्या है?

[End theme, 8 seconds.]

[Brand], [Campaign name]
Category: Regional Marketing. Market: Kerala. Period: August-September (Onam season).

[Brand] had to grow Kerala sales 15% in the Onam months. The insight: a hair oil is bought by one woman but remembered as a grandmother's hands. A Malayalam film and a WhatsApp sticker set put that ritual at the centre of Onam. Sales rose 22% while the category grew 6%.

1. CHALLENGE AND OBJECTIVES

Onam is the one festival the whole of Kerala shops for at the same time. For an Ayurveda hair-oil brand, the weeks around it are the window to win households, and every competitor knows it. Ayurveda oils tend to compete on herbs and heritage, claims that sound alike on a shelf and mean little to a shopper choosing in two seconds.

The brief we set ourselves was narrow: make [Brand] the oil Kerala families reach for in the Onam weeks, using a language and a ritual only Kerala shares.

Objective, set before launch: grow Kerala sales 15% in August-September against the same two months last year. Measured by retail audit, [audit agency], on the same panel as the category benchmark.

2. INSIGHT

We did not ask women what they want from a hair oil. We interviewed 40 consumers and asked about oiling itself: who did it, when, and what it felt like.

The answers skipped ingredients and went straight to grandmothers. Oiling came up as something done to you, by her, on a festival morning, with the whole family waiting their turn. It was remembered as the moment a busy house sat still. [Figure from the research deck: how many of the 40 named their grandmother unprompted.]

That is the human truth: the product is bought by one woman, but the ritual belongs to the whole family, and the grandmother is its author.

3. IDEA AND STRATEGY

The idea: let the grandmother say what the oil means, in Malayalam, at Onam.

The strategy followed from the insight. If the ritual is what people remember, the campaign should not explain the oil. It should return the ritual to the festival and let the brand sit inside it, in the grandmother's hands.

Two formats carried the idea. A Malayalam film told the ritual from the grandmother's side. A set of WhatsApp stickers, built from the phrases grandmothers use, let families pass the ritual to each other. Onam greetings in Kerala travel on WhatsApp, to cousins in other cities and relatives working away from home, so the stickers put the idea where the festival already happens.

4. EXECUTION

Timeline: [launch date] to [end date], built to land before Onam week and run through it.

The film: made in Malayalam for Kerala, not adapted from a national spot. Length [film length], released on [platforms]. The grandmother is the lead, the oil is the way she shows care, and the pack appears as part of the ritual rather than at the end of the film.

The stickers: [number] stickers in Malayalam, built from phrases grandmothers use at Onam, released as one pack that opens in a single tap. Seeded through [seeding plan].

Scale: [film views, source] and [stickers shared, source]. We report these as proof of reach only. The result that counts is sales.

5. RESULTS

Objective: grow Kerala sales 15% in August-September versus the same two months last year.

Result: Kerala sales grew 22%. Period: August-September. Source: retail audit, [audit agency]. That is 7 points above the objective. Put plainly: for every 100 units Kerala bought in August-September last year, it bought about 122 this year.

Benchmark: the category grew 6% over the same period, in the same audit. [Brand] grew 16 points faster than the market it sells in; the category moved from 100 to about 106.

Other factors we ruled out:
- Price: [no price cut or promotion in the period, confirm].
- Distribution: [no new outlets or distributor changes in Kerala, confirm].
- Seasonality: Onam falls inside August-September in both years [confirm], and the category's 6% is measured over the same festival window, so the festival lift is already in the benchmark.

Reach and conversation (film views, sticker shares) support the sales story but are not the claim. The claim is a 22% sales rise, in a festival every competitor was also selling into, from a ritual only a grandmother in Kerala would recognise.

Client permission to submit the audit data: [confirm in writing before the deadline].

samples.text:
COLLECTING OVERDUE INVOICES WITHOUT LOSING THE CLIENT
Chapter 2 of 5: The reminder ladder, three emails, one call and one escalation path

WHO THIS CHAPTER IS FOR

You run finance at a manufacturing company with Rs 20-200 crore in annual sales, and some of your customers pay when they feel like it. By the end of this chapter you will have three reminder emails ready to send and a phone script for invoices more than 60 days overdue. You will also have an escalation checklist your team can follow without asking you each time. You can start this month with email and a phone. No software is needed.

QUICK-START CHECKLIST

1. Export an ageing report by customer: current, 1-30, 31-60, 61-90 and 90+ days overdue.
2. Mark the ten largest overdue invoices and the five customers who owe the most in total.
3. Give every customer one named owner on your team. "Accounts" is not a name.
4. Confirm each invoice has its paperwork: PO, signed delivery challan or e-way bill, invoice.
5. Send Email 1 at 3 days after the due date.
6. Send Email 2 at 15 days, copying the salesperson who owns the account.
7. Send Email 3 at 30 days, signed by you.
8. Call at 60+ days using the script below, and write down the date the customer gives.
9. Confirm every call by email within the hour.
10. Escalate when a promised date is missed twice, using the checklist below.
11. Log every email, call and promised date in one shared sheet.
12. Review the sheet every Friday for 15 minutes.

WHY THIS STEP MATTERS

Most late payment is not a refusal. It is a missing PO number, an approval sitting with someone on leave, or a payment run that left without your invoice. A fixed ladder fixes those quickly and politely, and it leaves the relationship intact because the customer always knows what comes next. Chasing at random does the opposite: your team is soft in March, sharp in June, and the customer never learns what you actually expect.

HOW THE LADDER WORKS

Days are counted from the due date on the invoice.

1. Day 3: Email 1. Assume it was missed. Attach the documents.
2. Day 15: Email 2. Ask for a payment date, a UTR number or the reason it is held. Copy the salesperson.
3. Day 30: Email 3. Signed by the finance head. States what happens next.
4. Day 45: The salesperson phones the customer's buyer. This is a relationship call, not a collections call.
5. Day 60+: You phone the person who approves payment, using the script below.
6. Missed promised date, twice: run the escalation checklist.

EMAIL TEMPLATES

Replace the {braces}. Keep them short; a finance manager at the customer reads these between approvals.

EMAIL 1 (day 3)
Subject: Invoice {Invoice no.} for Rs {Amount}: due {Due date}

Dear {Name},

Our records show invoice {Invoice no.} dated {Invoice date}, for Rs {Amount}, was due on {Due date} and is still open. I have attached a copy with the PO and delivery challan.

If payment has gone out, please send the UTR number or cheque details so we can match it. If not, could you tell us the date it will be released?

Thank you,
{Your name}, Accounts, {Company}, {Direct phone}

EMAIL 2 (day 15)
Subject: Invoice {Invoice no.}: {Days} days overdue, payment date needed

Dear {Name},

Invoice {Invoice no.} for Rs {Amount} is now {Days} days past its due date of {Due date}. We have not had a reply to our note of {Date of Email 1}.

Please reply by {Date, 3 working days away} with one of three things: the payment date, the UTR number, or what is holding it up (quantity, quality or paperwork). If something is stopping payment, we would rather solve it this week than discuss it next month.

I have copied {Salesperson}, who looks after your account with us.

Regards,
{Your name}, {Direct phone}

EMAIL 3 (day 30)
Subject: Final reminder: invoice {Invoice no.}, Rs {Amount}, {Days} days overdue

Dear {Name},

This is our third reminder for invoice {Invoice no.} for Rs {Amount}, due on {Due date}. The total outstanding on your account is Rs {Total}, across {Number} invoices; the statement is attached.

We want to keep supplying you on current terms, and for that we need payment, or a written payment schedule, by {Date}. If we have not heard from you by then, I will call you on {Date + 1}, and we will review the credit terms on new orders.

Regards,
{Finance head}, {Company}, {Direct phone}
Cc: {Customer's finance head}, {Salesperson}

PHONE SCRIPT FOR 60+ DAYS OVERDUE

Before you dial: have the statement, invoice copies, PO, delivery proof and the email trail open. Decide in advance what you can offer: a split into two payments is fine, a waiver is not. Call the person who approves payment, not only the person who receives your emails.

1. Open (under 20 seconds). "Good morning {Name}, this is {You} from {Company}. Have you got five minutes? It is about {Number} invoices worth Rs {Total}, the oldest from {Date}. I wanted to speak to you directly instead of sending another mail."
2. Ask, then stay quiet. "What is holding these up on your side?" Let them finish.
3. Sort the answer.
   - A dispute: "Which invoice, and what exactly is the issue? I will check and come back by {Day}. Can the undisputed part be released meanwhile?"
   - A process delay: "Who has to approve, and when is the next payment run? I will send whatever they need today."
   - Cash is tight: "Can we split it, Rs {X} by {Date} and the balance by {Date}?"
   - A vague answer: "I understand. I need a date I can write down. Which date can you give me?"
4. Close with a commitment. "So we agree Rs {Amount} by {Date}, by NEFT or RTGS. I will confirm this by email within the hour."
5. After the call: send the confirming email, log the call, put the promised date in your calendar. If it is missed, call again the next working day.

Do not threaten, argue about why it is late, or mention stopping supply unless your MD has already decided it.

ESCALATION CHECKLIST

Use when a promised date has been missed twice, or an invoice passes 75 days with no reply.

- [ ] Paperwork complete: PO, signed delivery challan or e-way bill, acceptance or goods receipt, invoice, ledger statement.
- [ ] Dispute check: no open quality, quantity or rate query on this invoice.
- [ ] Contact log complete: three emails, the calls, every promised date.
- [ ] Sales head has called the customer's owner or MD.
- [ ] Supply decision made and signed off by your MD: hold, supply against advance, or continue.
- [ ] Your MD has written to the customer's MD, with the statement attached.
- [ ] If a cheque bounced: send the legal demand notice within 30 days of the bank's return memo, as Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act requires. The drawer then has 15 days to pay. [Confirm timelines with your counsel.]
- [ ] If your company is registered as a micro or small enterprise: ask counsel whether the MSMED Act's delayed-payment provisions apply. Ask also whether to file on the MSME Samadhaan portal.
- [ ] Legal notice drafted by counsel, with a decision date.
- [ ] Provision or write-off reviewed with your CFO or auditor at quarter end.

WORKED EXAMPLE (an illustration with assumed numbers, not a client case)

A manufacturer sells Rs 120 crore a year, about Rs 32.9 lakh a day (Rs 120 crore divided by 365). Its terms are 45 days, but customers actually pay at 68 days. That 23-day gap means about Rs 7.6 crore sits with customers beyond terms.

Run the ladder and bring the average to 58 days. Ten days earlier frees about Rs 3.3 crore (10 days x Rs 32.9 lakh). At an assumed 11% cost of working-capital borrowing, that is roughly Rs 36 lakh a year in interest saved, before counting a single new order. Replace these figures with your own from the ageing report; the arithmetic stays the same.

[Practitioner note, to be added: name, title and company of a finance head who moved from ad hoc calls to a fixed ladder, with their before-and-after days sales outstanding.]

WHAT USUALLY GOES WRONG

- Starting with Email 3. The customer's first message from you is a warning, and the relationship pays for it.
- Chasing from accounts@ with no name. Nobody owns the reply.
- Sending the reminder without the PO and delivery proof. The customer's payables team cannot pay what they cannot match.
- The salesperson saying "don't worry about it" to the buyer. Agree before you start that sales reinforces the ladder.
- Phoning only the buyer, who is not the approver. Ask in Email 2 who approves payment.
- No log. Every call starts from zero and the customer remembers the story better than you do.

DO THIS MONDAY

1. Monday morning: pull every invoice 31-90 days overdue from your ageing report. Give each a named owner and a next ladder step.
2. By Wednesday: send Email 2 or Email 3 to each, depending on age.
3. By Friday: book the 60+ day calls for next week, 15 minutes each, with the script open.
4. Week 3: run the escalation checklist on every invoice that missed two promised dates.
5. Week 4: sit with the sheet. How much was collected, what is stuck and with whom, and what is your average payment day now?

NEXT STEP

Run the ladder by hand for four weeks and you will see which part eats your team's time. [Product] sends these three emails on schedule from your ledger, logs every reply and flags the invoices that reach day 60 so the call lands on your desk. To see it on your own ageing report, book a 20-minute walkthrough at [link]. Chapter 3 picks up from here.

Last updated: 6 Oct 2026. Owner: [name, Product Marketing]. Review each quarter and after any price change. Sources: [X's public pricing page, X's website, G2 reviews, dates].

WE WIN ON
Statutory compliance automation (PF, ESI and professional tax across states) and WhatsApp payslips, with 50-500 employee Indian companies and a one- or two-person HR team.

QUICK FACTS ABOUT X
- Segment: national payroll provider; [segments they target, from their site].
- Pricing: prospects tell us X is cheaper. [X's list price per employee per month, source, date.]
- Strengths: bigger brand, payroll bundled with accounting.
- Recent changes: [latest pricing or product change, source, date].

WHY WE WIN
- Compliance across states. PT slabs and due dates differ by state; we keep PF, ESI and PT current, so your team does not run them from a spreadsheet. Proof: [named customer, states covered, filings handled].
- WhatsApp payslips. Plant, field and shift staff who never open email get their payslip on the phone they already check. Proof: [delivery or open rate, source].
- Built for 50-500 employees. Set-up and support are sized for a small HR team. Proof: [named customer at this size, approved].

WHERE X IS STRONG (say so, then qualify)
- Brand size. True; do not dispute it. Ask what the brand is protecting them from, then go to compliance.
- Bundled accounting. A real advantage for a buyer who wants one vendor. Qualify first: who keeps the books today, and would they change?
- Lower quote. It may be. Compare what each quote includes, not the headline price.

FOUR TRAP QUESTIONS
1. Which states do your people work in, and who tracks each state's professional tax slabs and due dates today?
2. When a PF or ESI rule changes, who spots it first, and how long until payroll reflects it?
3. How do your plant and field staff get their payslip now, and how many of them check email?
4. If payroll and accounts sat in separate systems, what would actually break?

THEY SAY / YOU SAY / PROOF

1. They say: "X is much bigger than you."
You say: "They are, and for many buyers that is reassuring. What does the size do for you on a Tuesday when a state changes its PT slab? Compliance across states is what we are strongest at for companies your size."
Proof: [named switch story].

2. They say: "X is cheaper."
You say: "It may be on the first page of the quote. Can we put both quotes side by side: PF, ESI and PT in every state you operate in, payslip delivery, and your payroll person's hours? I would rather you compare the whole cost than pick the lower number."
Proof: [hours saved, customer, source].

3. They say: "X gives us payroll and accounting together."
You say: "If one vendor matters most, tell me; that is a genuine plus. Who keeps your books today, and what would they need from payroll each month?"
Proof: [integration or export we support, confirmed with Product].

4. They say: "Email payslips are fine."
You say: "For the office, yes. What about the people who work on the shop floor and the road? WhatsApp reaches them on the phone they already open."
Proof: [open rate, source].

5. They say: "Switching payroll is risky."
You say: "It is, so we plan it before anyone's salary moves. [Our migration steps, confirmed with Onboarding.]"
Proof: [named switch story, go-live date].

NEVER SAY
- That X is non-compliant, error-prone or unreliable. We cannot verify it.
- X's price, unless it is on their public page with a date.
- That we have a feature or integration that Product has not confirmed.
- A discount, on the first call. Run the side-by-side cost comparison first; any discount after it needs manager approval.

PROOF TO USE
- Named switch stories: [customer, size, states, result, approved].
- Anonymised, only if approved: [customer type, size, result].

META TITLE: Monsoon-Proofing a Kerala Home: 7 Checks Before June
META DESCRIPTION: Seven checks to do before the monsoon reaches Kerala, from terrace parapet joints to bathroom slabs and window sills. Book a free site inspection in Kochi.

Monsoon-proofing a Kerala home: 7 checks to do before June

Walk your house in May and check seven places. They are the terrace parapet joints, the terrace drains, the bathroom slab, the window sills, the outer walls, the rainwater path around the house and the electrical points near water. Fix what you find before the monsoon, which normally reaches Kerala around 1 June. A leak found in July costs more and takes longer to fix.

We're a home-renovation company in Kochi, and this list comes from what our site crew repairs every rainy season. The parapet joints, the bathroom slab and the window sills are the three leak points they fix most. Under each check you'll find what to look for, what you can do yourself, and when to call someone.

## Are the terrace parapet joints cracked?

Look along the line where the parapet wall meets the terrace slab. If you can slide a fingernail into a gap, or see a hairline crack, water will find it.

This is one of the three places our crew fixes most. A parapet joint is where two parts of the house meet, and they don't expand and shrink at the same rate. The crack opens a little every summer, and the first heavy rain finds it. The stain often shows up on the ceiling or wall below, a few feet from the actual crack, because water travels along the slab before it drips.

[Photo: a cracked parapet joint from a recent Kochi site, with locality and date.]

What to do: clear the moss and dirt, open any crack with a chisel and seal it. Then have the junction finished with a rounded mortar fillet and waterproof coating carried up the parapet wall. Our guide to [terrace waterproofing for Kerala homes](link) explains the options.

Then run a ponding test. Block the drain outlets, hold a few centimetres of water on the terrace for at least 24 hours, and check the ceiling below. Unblock the outlets afterwards.

## Are the terrace drains clear?

Clear every outlet and downpipe before June, then pour a bucket of water near each one. It should drain in seconds, not pool.

Coconut fronds, areca leaves and plastic collect at outlets through the dry months. Water that sits on a terrace for days finds every small crack, including ones that were fine in a short shower. While you're up there, check that the slab slopes towards the outlets. A puddle that stays after the rain stops is a slope fault, and that needs more than a broom.

## Is water coming through the bathroom slab?

Look at the ceiling of the room below the bathroom, and at any wall the bathroom shares. A stain, peeling paint or a damp smell means the slab or the pipe sleeves are leaking.

Our crew sees this leak point again and again. In the monsoon, humid air stops damp patches from drying, so a slow leak that stayed hidden in summer starts to show as a stain. Check the gaps around the waste-pipe collars and the grout lines at the floor edge.

What to do: re-grouting buys a few weeks, not a season. A leak under the tiles usually means lifting them and redoing the waterproofing layer. That's not a weekend job, so book it before the rain, not during it. If you're renovating the bathroom anyway, ask for [bathroom waterproofing done as part of the renovation](link).

## Are the window sills sealed and sloping outward?

Run your hand along each sill and the joint between the sill and the frame. A gap wider than a hairline, or a sill that slopes into the room, will let wind-driven rain in.

Window sills are the third place our crew fixes most. Seal gaps with a flexible exterior sealant, not cement, which cracks as the frame moves. The sill should slope outward, with a drip groove under its outer edge so water falls clear of the wall instead of running back along it. Stained plaster under a window is the usual sign that this has already been going on for a season or two.

[Quote from the site supervisor, name and role: one line on what they find at window sills.]

## Do the outer walls have cracks that let rain in?

Walk around the house and look for cracks wider than a hairline, especially at corners, above windows and where a wall meets a column.

Rain on a south-west-facing wall is driven hard in June and July. A crack that looks cosmetic in May lets water into the plaster by July. Fill it with a crack filler or flexible sealant first. Paint comes after, not instead: a fresh coat over an open crack hides it for a month. If a wall has several cracks, our team can look at [exterior wall repair and painting](link) before you commit to a repaint.

## Is rainwater leaving the roof and the plot?

Check where the water goes after it leaves the roof. Downpipes should discharge away from the house, the drain around the plinth should be open, and the soil by the wall should slope away from it.

If you have a sloped tile roof, look for slipped or cracked tiles and clear the valley gutters. Clogged gutters send water over the edge and down the wall, which is how a roof problem becomes a wall problem. It takes one ladder and one afternoon; go up with another person holding it.

## Are your electrical points safe in a damp house?

Press the test button on your RCCB (the earth-leakage breaker in the fuse box). It should trip at once. If it doesn't, call a licensed electrician before June.

Also look at outdoor switchboards and bathroom points for rust, damp or a stained wall behind them. Damp near wiring is the one problem on this list that can hurt someone, so don't wait for a stain to spread. If a socket sparks or a switchboard feels warm, switch it off at the main and call an electrician.

## The checklist, in order

- Terrace parapet joints: look, seal, ponding test.
- Terrace drains: clear every outlet and pour a bucket of water.
- Bathroom slab: check the room below for stains and damp.
- Window sills: seal gaps, confirm the slope and the drip groove.
- Outer walls: fill cracks before you paint.
- Roof and plot: downpipes, plinth drain, tiles and gutters.
- Electrical: test the RCCB and check outdoor points.

## Want someone to check it with you?

We'll walk the house with you and tell you what needs fixing before June. The inspection is free. [Book a free site inspection](link) or WhatsApp us on [number]. We cover [Kochi and nearby areas, confirm].
